items.title: [ScienceDaily] Strokes have nearly doubled among younger adults, and scientists aren't sure why
items.content_html:
🏔️ ✏️

Strokes are becoming alarmingly common among younger adults, with rates nearly doubling among people ages 20 to 54 over nearly three decades. Researchers found that blocked blood vessels in the brain accounted for much of the increase, while high blood pressure, diabetes, and substance use also became more common among younger stroke patients. Although survival rates have improved, more young adults may now face the lasting consequences of stroke.

items.title: [Fast Company] Half of the world’s population has been exposed to heat waves and wildfire smoke at the same time
items.content_html:
🏔️ ✏️

Climate change is a global phenomenon, meaning that everyone, in some way, will feel its devastating impacts. 

And increasingly, those impacts are happening simultaneously: Over the past two decades, more than half of the world’s population has experienced simultaneous heat waves and wildfires, occurring on the same day, a study found.

Researchers at Monash University in Melbourne, Australia, published their findings this week in the journal Science Advances.

The study looked at 20 years of data, from 2000 to 2019. To see who experienced a wildfire, researchers looked at who was exposed to “fire-sourced air pollution”; their data took into account hourly temperature, fire emissions, air quality, and population information.

Over those 20 years, researchers found, the number of people around the world exposed to both wildfires and heat waves, on the same days, increased by 287 million—from 761 million people per year in the first half of that time period to more than 1 billion people per year in the second.

That means 55.9% of the global population has experienced at least one day where a heat wave and wildfire pollution occurred in tandem.

And the number of such days is increasing. From 2000 to 2009, the average person experienced one such day per year. Between 2010 and 2019, that rose to 1.7 days of co-exposure per person.

Damaging on multiple levels

The research doesn’t only illustrate how climate change is making extreme weather more frequent. It also shows how the health impacts of these events can compound as extreme weather overlaps.

Both heat waves and wildfires can cause serious harm to our health. Along with the risk of heatstroke—which can damage your brain, heart, and kidneys, and even be fatal—extreme heat and humidity can make it harder for some people to breathe, especially those with asthma or other lung conditions. 

Wildfires come with intense air pollution, full of tiny particles called PM2.5 (particulate matter 2.5 micrometers or less in diameter) that can get into our lungs and bloodstream, raising the risk of heart attack, stroke, and reduced lung function.

When heat waves combine with air pollution, the health impacts exacerbate. On days when an area sees a “double whammy” of high heat and high air pollution, the risk of death is three times greater “than the effect of either high heat or high air pollution alone,” health researchers have previously written. 

The Monash University researchers emphasize this in their study, too. “Compared with exposure to heat wave or landscape fire-sourced air pollution alone, co-exposure to both hazards may exert greater health impacts than the sum of their individual effects,” they write. 

In other words, the health risks—including respiratory and cardiovascular impacts—become amplified when wildfire air pollution and extreme heat happen together.

Extreme heat and wildfires also impact each event occurring. Conditions like high temperatures and dry soil promote wildfires, and wildfires then exacerbate heat waves because they release heat and pollution into the air.

“These processes create a positive feedback loop in which heat waves and fires amplify one another,” the researchers wrote.

Which regions are being hit hardest?

Some regions of the world are experiencing these simultaneous effects more than others. Zambia, for example, sees more than 28 such days per person every year. The Democratic Republic of the Congo comes in second, with just over 24 days per person per year.

Countries with lower life expectancy, education, and income tended to see the highest amount of wildfire and heat co-exposure, an example of the way that climate change is hitting the world’s poorest countries the hardest. 

Still, almost every area of the world saw an increase in this trend.

Central America, South America, Central and Eastern Africa, Southeast Asia, and parts of North America, Australia, and Russia all experienced “notable increases” in the annual average number of days that wildfire pollution and extreme heat occurred together.

items.title: [Fast Company] Dementia cases are expected to more than double by 2050. A new study reveals who’s most at risk
items.content_html:
🏔️ ✏️

More and more of our loved ones could develop dementia, as the number of diagnoses is projected to more than double by 2050, according to new research.

In the absence of large-scale prevention efforts, the number of people who are diagnosed with dementia each year could total 24.7 million by 2050, up from 11.4 million in 2023, according to a study by Australian researchers published in JAMA Neurology. Women and people who live in low- and middle-income countries already have higher rates of dementia, a trend that’s likely to continue, according to the findings.

While the researchers didn’t pinpoint an exact reason why dementia affects populations differently, they say the prospect of more cases warrants urgency in investing in prevention efforts. The prospect of 24 million new cases of dementia each year would place “enormous pressure on individuals, families, health systems and economies around the world,” Henry Brodaty, co-director of the Centre for Healthy Brain Ageing at the University of New South Wales Sydney and a co-author of the study, said in a statement.

“We cannot simply wait for people to develop dementia and then respond,” Brodaty said. “We need to act across the spectrum—from reducing modifiable risk factors and identifying people at risk earlier, through to improving diagnosis, treatment and care.”

The researchers studied data from more than 38,000 people diagnosed with dementia spanning 18 countries or territories on six continents. They found that the incidence was somewhat higher among women—at 10.6 cases per 1,000 people versus 8.6 for men—but the difference was even starker depending on where people lived. The incidence of dementia was 13.6 cases per 1,000 people in low- and middle-income countries, compared with 8.3 in high-income countries.

Understanding the populations who are most at-risk for developing dementia will be key to developing prevention, diagnosis and care strategies, according to the study’s authors. 

“The higher incidence we observed in low- and middle-income countries is particularly concerning because these regions are experiencing rapid population aging while often having the fewest resources for prevention, diagnosis and care,” Perminder Sachdev, co-director of the Centre for Healthy Brain Ageing at the University of New South Wales in Sydney and a senior author of the study, said.

THE FINANCIAL TOLL OF DEMENTIA

Aging populations are understandably one of the main reasons why dementia cases are expected to increase, as this condition that affects memory, thinking and the ability to perform daily activities is more common after the age of 65. As of 2021, an estimated 57 million people worldwide were living with dementia, according to figures from the World Health Organization, and it’s the seventh leading cause of death.

The World Health Organization likewise estimated that as of 2019, dementia cost economies around the world about $1.3 trillion, so a surge in new cases also carries a financial toll. 

That’s why the new research should sound an alarm, as Dr. Liron Sinvani, director of research and innovation at the Northwell Institute for Healthy Aging and a professor at the Feinstein Institutes for Medical Research in New York, told U.S. News & World Report. “It’s an accelerating epidemic that demands immediate attention.” 

And that’s especially important as the countries that will face an “enormous wave” of dementia cases also have very limited infrastructure to respond, as Sinvani told the outlet. 

“Health systems must prepare for this massive increase in diagnostic and care demand, and this is especially true for these low- and middle-income countries where the growth will be fastest,” she said. “We know that dementia care requires a lot of caregiver support and is very costly. We will need a better infrastructure.”

items.title: [zive.aktuality.sk] Century-old Isle of Wight fossil reveals Europe's first megaraptoran
items.content_html:
🏔️ ✏️

Researchers have identified a new predatory dinosaur, Invictibellatrix amberina, from a skull fragment found on the Isle of Wight, making it the first known megaraptoran found in Europe. The animal lived about 120 million years ago and was likely 3 to 4 metres long, with powerful forelimbs and curved claws estimated at 10 to 20 centimetres [sciencedaily.com#1][sci.news#1][cbsnews.com#2]. The Natural History Museum acquired the fossil in 1924, but it remained undescribed until a team led by University College London examined it. The discovery supports a proposed route in which megaraptorans spread from Asia through Europe to Gondwana, rather than reaching the southern continents by island-hopping. The researchers published the study in Royal Society Open Science on October 14, 2026 [sci.news#1][aawsat.com#1][sciencedaily.com#1].
